claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a disordered BCC solid solution at room temperature.
The specimens are fully homogenized, cold-rolled, and annealed before testing.
Room-temperature deformation in HfNbTaTiZr is dominated by screw dislocations.
Heating HfNbTaTiZr causes deformation to transition from screw-dislocation-dominated motion to edge-dislocation-dominated motion.
Elevated temperature induces local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Temperature-induced local lattice distortions activate alternative slip modes and facilitate edge-dislocation motion.
Thermal activation lowers the effective barrier for edge-dislocation motion.
Yield strength decreases with increasing temperature before the proposed edge-dislocation transition.
Activation and eventual dominance of edge dislocations produce a plateau in elevated-temperature yield strength.
The dislocation-mode transition modifies the elastic moduli of HfNbTaTiZr.
The dislocation-mode transition modifies the thermal-expansion coefficient of HfNbTaTiZr.
In-situ diffraction will reveal altered lattice-distortion patterns consistent with increased edge-dislocation activity.
Dislocation slip controls plastic deformation in a compositionally related NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 refractory alloy.
A screw-to-edge slip-mode transition has produced a medium-temperature strength plateau in other refractory high-entropy alloys.
The hypothesis is proposed to hold from 600°C to 1200°C under inert atmosphere and constant strain rate.
Room-temperature measurements provide the control baseline for the elevated-temperature tests.
Yield strength, plasticity, elastic moduli, lattice parameters, dislocation character, and thermal expansion will be measured as functions of temperature.

The hypothesis is falsified if both the proposed dislocation transition or associated lattice-distortion change is absent and plateau behavior is absent from the strength or elastic response over 600°C–1200°C.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome assigns plateau behavior specifically to strength and predicts only measurable changes in elastic moduli, whereas the falsification rule appears to require plateau behavior in both yield strength and elastic moduli.
